hints: Notice the order lamp, then single slit, then double slit: the lamp filament emits light with random, rapidly changing phase.
Recall that two-source interference on the screen needs the two slits to act as coherent sources with constant phase difference.
Think how diffraction at one narrow slit can turn extended incoherent light into a single wavefront that illuminates both slits of the double slit.
walkthrough: Identify the problem: the filament lamp is an extended source where different points emit with random phase, so the double slit would not by itself give stable interference.
State the rule: observable two-source fringes need coherent waves, meaning same frequency and constant phase difference, so that path difference controls constructive and destructive superposition.
Consider the single slit: light through it diffracts and spreads out from an effectively single narrow source before reaching the double slit.

Because both slits of the double slit are then lit by the same single wavefront, any phase change at the single slit affects both equally and the phase difference between the double slits stays constant.
A colour filter would select wavelength and symmetric illumination would balance amplitude, but neither creates coherence. This is option C.

options.A: A narrow beam alone does not create the fixed phase relationship needed for stable interference fringes on the screen.
options.B: Equal illumination helps fringe contrast but the essential requirement for the double slit is a constant phase difference.
options.C: Diffraction at the single slit creates effectively one source, so waves reaching the two slits of the double slit have a constant phase difference.
options.D: A filament lamp with a single slit is still white light; a colour filter or laser would be needed for monochromatic light.
